text.p: The Federal Reserve Board Wednesday knocked down some barriers between banks and their securities affiliates, which bankers saw as a step toward allowing one-stop shopping for various financial products.
The Fed loosened three "firewalls" designed to keep banks at arm's length from their bank holding companies' securities subsidiaries.
Now banks will be able to share employees with the securities affiliate and market the products of the securities units.
A bank will also be allowed to buy and sell for its own account a wider array of securities in transactions with its securities affiliate.
"The Fed has taken one more step to allow banks to act more like securities firms," said Larry LaRocco, managing director of the American Bankers Association's securities association.
"It simply means that your banker will now have access to more securities products, have a wider array of financial products for (customers)," he added.
Thirty-nine bank holding companies have securities subsidiaries, known as "section 20" subsidiaries after the section of the Glass-Steagall Act that allowed their creation.
The Depression-era Glass-Steagall law separates commercial and investment banking.

A key proposal still under consideration at the Fed would expand the amount of activity that section 20 subsidiaries are permitted in securities such as corporate bonds, stocks and municipal revenue bonds. That proposal would allow a securities subsidiary to derive 25 percent of total revenue from those activities, up from the current 10 percent limit.
The comment period for that proposal ended September 30. Bankers guessed the Fed may take it up next month.
Congressional efforts to repeal the Glass-Steagall law fell through earlier this year, and Fed officials continued to say repeal was needed.
"I hope we get rid of the legislation, but absent that this is a very good (proposal)," Fed Governor Susan Phillips said at the meeting Wednesday.
The Fed's action Wednesday would result in cost savings for banks and could encourage more banks to seek securities affiliates, banking groups said.
A bank and its securities affiliate will now be able to share employees, rather than each hiring individuals with expertise in the same areas.

However, a bank's chief executive officer would still be prohibited from occupying that position at the securities affiliate, and directors and officers of a bank would not be allowed to serve as a majority of the board of directors of the securities subsidiary, the Fed said.
The Fed's repeal of "cross-marketing" restrictions would allow a bank to market the products of the securities subsidiary.

"I think probably the biggest dividend of this will be to the customer, who will now be able to deal with one person ... or at least a team ... that can meet the customer's needs through an array of products," Richard Whiting, general counsel for The Bankers Roundtable, said.
The third restriction that was loosened dealt with purchases and sales of securities for the bank's own account through transactions between the bank and its securities affiliate.
Previously U.S. Treasury securities were allowed for such transactions, and now any security with a broad and liquid market, purchased at the publicly-available market quotation, would be permitted.
